title: 100-0 Denied: Bullet Grandpa Beats Dubov In Game 28
summary:
Arizona businessman and amateur chess player Josh Smith (@BulletGrandpa) won a single game against super-GM Daniil Dubov in the final match of the 100-0 Project Season 1 to prevent a super-adoption. The question was whether a super-grandmaster can beat an amateur in 100 consecutive bullet games without a single draw. Smith won game 28, though Dubov won all 99 of the other games.

Dubov earned $10,000 for participating, but not the $20,000 promised for winning the match. IM Danny Rensch also announced Season 2 will take place from December 2026 to March 2027, culminating in a match against final boss GM Levon Aronian.

Greg Mustreader and Smith created the 100-0 Project to pit an amateur bullet enthusiast against world-class opposition in a match that can, in theory, go either way. "Can the absolute best players in the world beat me 100-0?" asked the Bullet Grandpa, who is 49 years old, in the video trailer. The answer, at least in the first edition, is no.

Smith had prepared for months ahead of the final boss, Dubov. From September through October, he played 50-game matches against many content creators and chess personalities. As you can see in the table below, he wasn't swept in any of them, even by GMs Arturs Neiksans or Vasif Durarbayli.

While the training matches consisted of 50 games, the final match was 100. The time control was 1+0, the standard for "pure" bullet.

On October 6, Bullet Grandpa—who estimates he's played over 250,000 bullet games—had set his record of 2579 rating in bullet chess, but he started this match with a 2424 rating. Dubov was at a monstrous 3225. The grandmaster won the first 27 games with several sacrifices and brilliant moves along the way.

Dubov's vast opening knowledge, even of dubious lines, was on full display in this match—and even with just a minute, he converted advantages with brutal precision. Game three was a good example of Dubov winning right out of the opening against a Czech Benoni. After 9.Bb5+, there's no good move to recommend for Black. He fell apart.

The first nine games were all one-sided. Game six was a 16-move miniature that Dubov won with the black pieces. The attack started with the pawn sacrifice 7...e3! to open up the white king.

Efficiency is key in bullet chess, as you want to win quickly to avoid even the possibility of losing on time. Dubov hardly got into time trouble, and 40.f3 in the next game is a good example of Dubov's incisive conversion. The game ended with a satisfying checkmate just one move later.

Game 10 is the closest Smith got to holding a draw in the early stage, but trading into the knight endgame allowed Dubov to take over in an equal-material endgame with the more active king.

One of the biggest fears for Dubov must have been a mouse slip. We did see a mouse slip in game 14, but as GM Kayden Troff (Smith's coach) announced, "The first mouse slip, but not for Dubov!"

In game 15, Dubov's queen sacrifice 27.Qc6!! is one of the best moves of the day. If the queen is captured, 28.Rb8 is checkmate.

In game 24, Smith outplayed Dubov briefly but went on to lose control in the rook and opposite-color bishop endgame. The grandmaster went on to win with a rare checkmate, strangely ending the game with a king move!

Every 25 games, the players took a break. So three games after the first break, Smith had already decided the match. In game 28, Smith hung his queen, Dubov didn't see it and hung his bishop in return, and the amateur went on to win in the time scramble.

Josh Smith hangs his queen, but Dubov doesn't see it and blunders a bishop in return! Smith is now winning! https://t.co/BPb9w8FO0t https://t.co/EH6re6YTAQ

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 7, 2026

Celebrating the victory, Bullet Grandpa yelled out, "He's human!"

"He's human! He bleeds!" The Bullet Grandpa celebrates as he wins game 28, so Dubov is unable to win 100-0! https://t.co/MpFf1h5pdS

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 7, 2026

Although the experiment was effectively over, the players continued the match and played out the rest of the games. The lowered stakes may have helped Dubov loosen up, and he surprised even himself with the 99-1 final score. He said he expected 97-3 or even 95-5. "There were two or three games where I was lucky chess-wise," he said, referring to games he saved on time rather than by the strength of his moves. The following clip shows one of those games:

The Bullet Grandpa nearly wins a second game, but Dubov slips away and wins! https://t.co/Ros1zuiN6d

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 7, 2026

Smith, after denying the sweep, said, "I was just blown away. I've never played a super-elite player of Dubov's caliber before, and I have incredible respect for his tactics." He said the match was even more difficult than he thought it would be. And he explained: "I run out of ideas. I run out of moves, and it feels so hopeless, but I try to come up with certain things, but it's so easy to put you up on a pedestal and say that you're [Dubov] just inhuman, that you're just a robot."

I was just blown away. I've never played a super-elite player of Dubov's caliber before.

—Josh Smith

Dubov responded, "It's not about a pedestal or whatever. It's just you've gotta wait for this blunder, and this blunder will come for sure. And there will be like five games where you get a chance, or maybe more games actually."

You've gotta wait for this blunder, and this blunder will come for sure. And there will be like five games where you get a chance, or maybe more games actually.

—Daniil Dubov's advice for Smith

As the Bullet Grandpa prepares for Season 2, which will feature a final match against Aronian, he will have to think hard about his openings with White. Dubov explained he'd watched some of the training matches and recommended playing those in secret next time. He identified a pattern: Smith likes to play, regardless of move orders, the moves d4, Nf3, b3, Bb2, g3, Bg2—that kind of setup, which you can easily premove. Dubov trusted he'd get better positions with White every game, but he did work on countering this setup with Black.

Can the Bullet Grandpa do it again, against Levon Aronian? Let us know your Season 2 predictions in the comments below!

How to review?

You can review the event on the Chess24 Twitch or YouTube pages. You can also check out The Bullet Grandpa on YouTube.

The live broadcast was hosted by GM Kayden Troff and Greg Mustreader.

An amateur bullet enthusiast from Arizona took on a gauntlet of streamers and masters in epic matches, all building toward one shot at super-GM Daniil Dubov. The final match, taking place on November 7 on Chess.com, was a 100-game match with a 1+0 time control per game. Winning all 100 games would have earned Dubov the full $20,000 prize, while a single draw for the Bullet Grandpa would have resulted in Dubov earning just $10,000.

title: Janak Awatramani Wins His 2nd Crazyhouse Championship
summary:
NM Janak Awatramani beat GM Guillermo Vazquez 3-0 in the Grand Final to win the 2026 Crazyhouse Championship, following up on his victory in 2024. Crazyhouse, as commentator GM Yasser Seirawan mentioned, is often called "Bughouse for one player," so it's perhaps no surprise that Awatramani has won the last two Bughouse championships as well. He did that together with NM Isaac Chiu, who took the Crazyhouse title in 2025, but this time Awatramani won their Winners Final clash 3-1.

The next Chess.com Community Championship, on December 17-18, is the 2026 Fog Of War Championship.

Final Bracket

What Is Crazyhouse?

Qualifiers: Awonder Liang Drops Out

Knockout: Awatramani Storms To Title

What Is Crazyhouse?

Crazyhouse follows the same pattern as Bughouse in that captured pieces can return to the board, but it's a game for two players instead of four. Rather than passing a piece to your partner, you can choose to place it on the board yourself instead of moving another piece. Here are the rules that differ from normal chess.

When you capture an opponent's piece, it is placed in your "pool" of pieces, and you can "drop" it on an empty square on your turn.

Pieces may only be dropped on empty squares.

You may drop a piece to give check or checkmate.

Pawns may not be dropped on the first or eighth ranks.

It follows that you can get unusual piece arrangements, such as a four-bishop defensive setup!

The value of the initiative is huge, since an attack fuels itself as you capture and re-add pieces. There are essentially no endgames—since pieces return to the board—and draws are rare, but they can be amusing when they do occur! (This one is from 2025.)

Draws are rare in Crazyhouse, but Yasser explains how you make them! pic.twitter.com/g5VDTo7LuT

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 7, 2025

The Chess.com Crazyhouse Championship featured eight arena qualifiers followed by an eight-player final tournament.

Qualifiers: Awonder Liang Drops Out

Thursday saw eight qualifiers, which players of all levels could register for. They were 75-minute arenas with a 3+0 time control and produced the following eight qualifiers, including three Canadians.

The highest winning score was 123 points for IM Mark Plotkin, who once went on a 19-game winning streak. The lowest winning score was 60 points, for Justin Tan, but that was also one of the most welcome qualifications. "JannLee" is a Crazyhouse legend who has won previous Chess.com Championships and is often considered the "first world champion" of the game.

Some top players missed out, including GM Jeffery Xiong, who was second to Chiu in the first qualifier, and Seirawan, who twice finished fifth. That loss was the audience's gain, since he once again teamed up with GM Benjamin Bok to provide commentary.

The one disappointment is that GM Awonder Liang, the winner of the preceding Seirawan Chess Championship, qualified as the winner of the fourth arena but then was unable to play in the Finals. His spot would have gone to second-placed Vazquez, but as the Paraguayan GM won the next arena, it went to third-placed Brendan Cater instead.

Knockout: Awatramani Storms To Title

Three players won 3-0 in the opening matches of the Quarterfinals, but the remaining match was a thriller. Tan got off to a powerful start, taking a 2-0 lead against Chiu. The defending champion fought back, however, winning the next two games.

The second of those saw him dominate on the clock, but also finish off with checkmate on the board. There was only one good way to react to a pawn being dropped on h2, and Tan didn't find it.

Defending Crazyhouse Champion Isaac Chiu fights back from 2-0 down to force a decider! https://t.co/pjuZb8MBxM https://t.co/zVQ2fChGvM

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 6, 2026

Chiu went on to win the bullet decider convincingly, but Tan got to fight on in the Losers bracket.

He beat Cater 3-0 and then was only stopped 3-2 by FM Roee Aroesti (Crazy_Eight) in the Losers Quarterfinals. That finished in dramatic fashion, as Tan was down on time in the bullet decider but had mate-in-two on the board.

Down to under two seconds, Tan went astray here, but he could have grabbed the bishop on d4 with check and then dropped that bishop on a4 with checkmate next move!

Aroesti is the player who gave the eventual winner his toughest match, with Awatramani losing the first game of the Winners Semifinals from a completely winning position. He had to put a piece on f3—preventing Black from doing the same—and when he grabbed a rook on c8 instead, disaster followed. It's amazing how fast things can turn around in Crazyhouse.

Awatramani hit back to win the next two games, then lost again, but won in bullet with the white pieces.

That set up a Winners Final against his Bughouse partner Chiu, with Awatramani scoring an impressive 3-1 victory, though Chiu's win was perhaps the most memorable game of the match. Black's four rooks should have been more than enough to win, but one mistake led to a nice smothered mate.

So Awatramani was in the Grand Final, but who would he face? In the end, it came down to a hard-fought battle between Chiu and Vazquez. Vazquez took the lead twice, the second time in the most dramatic fashion possible—Chiu had mate-in-five in the final position, but didn't manage to make a move in 0.9 seconds against his opponent's single second.

Chiu hit back both times, however, and lost only in the bullet decider.

That meant a potentially thrilling final battle between the one grandmaster in the field, Vazquez, and Awatramani. In the end, however, it was anticlimactic—Awatramani blew his opponent away in 19 moves in game one, then was on top for almost all of game two before delivering mate-in-four.

The final must-win game for Vazquez had some swings, but Awatramani had the advantage for most of the encounter and finished things off nicely in a demonstration of how the material that's on the board in Crazyhouse can be very deceptive.

Congratulations to Canadian NM Janak Awatramani on clinching victory in the Crazyhouse Championship with a 3-0 win in the Grand Final! 🏆 https://t.co/tCpUQzXk82

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 6, 2026

Awatramani picked up the $750 top prize, with the top three also gifted a special set of 3D-printed Crazyhouse pieces (flip them to change their color) from our very own NM Sam Copeland.

There's now just one Community Championship left before the end of the year—the 2026 Fog Of War Championship on December 17-18. Once again, it's open to everyone, so don't miss out!

How to review?

You can review the 2026 Chess.com Community Championships: Crazyhouse on the Chess.com Twitch or YouTube pages.

The live broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan and Benjamin Bok.

The 2026 Crazyhouse Chess Championship is the 11th event of the 2026 Chess.com Community Championship series. Winners of eight qualifiers (each was a 75-minute arena with a 3+0 time control) entered the Final on November 6, which was an eight-player double-elimination bracket. The time control was 3+0, and matches were best-of-four. The total prize fund was $2,500.

title: The young king faces his toughest challenge
summary: From prodigious talent to the youngest World Champion in history, Gukesh Dommaraju has enjoyed a meteoric rise to the summit of the chess world. Now, as he prepares to defend his crown against Uzbekistan’s rising star Javokhir Sindarov, the Indian prodigy faces perhaps the greatest challenge of his career: rediscovering his best form. World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju embodies ambition, determination and youthful excellence. His remarkable rise to the pinnacle of the chess world, marked by record-breaking achievements and historic milestones, is an extraordinary story of talent, perseverance and self-belief. At just 18 years of age, he achieved what generations of chess players can only dream of: becoming the youngest undisputed World Champion in history. Born on 29 May 2006 in Chennai, the same city that nurtured India’s chess legend Viswanathan Anand, Gukesh showed signs of exceptional talent from an early age. Having learned the rules of chess at the age of seven, he quickly demonstrated a natural aptitude for the game, winning the Asian School Chess Championships in 2015. Soon afterwards, he left formal schooling to devote himself entirely to chess. With the unwavering support of his parents, Gukesh continued to develop his skills, becoming an International Master in 2017. His training approach placed particular emphasis on independent thinking and understanding positions rather than relying on chess engines. This helped him develop a distinctive playing style and strong analytical abilities. In January 2019, at the age of just 12 years, seven months and 17 days, he became the second-youngest grandmaster in chess history. Photo: John Saunders His progress continued at an impressive pace. After collecting medals at international youth championships, Gukesh spent the Covid period further strengthening his game, and competed both online and over the board.Another breakthrough came at the 2022 Chess Olympiad in Chennai, where he represented India’s second team, helping it secure the bronze medal. Individually, he produced a spectacular performance on the first board, scoring 9 points out of 11 and winning the individual gold medal. Further outstanding results in 2022 and 2023 propelled him into the world’s elite. He became the youngest player ever to surpass the 2750 Elo rating mark and qualified for the 2024 Candidates Tournament. Held in April, this prestigious competition brought together eight of the world’s strongest players to determine the challenger to reigning World Champion Ding Liren. Gukesh once again made history by becoming the youngest Candidates winner ever. Photo: Michal Walusza September 2024 brought another landmark achievement for Indian chess. At the Chess Olympiad in Budapest, India claimed its first-ever gold medal. Gukesh played a central role in this historic triumph, winning the individual gold medal on Board 1 with an outstanding score of 9 points out of 10 and a stellar rating performance of 3056. This result also propelled him into the world’s top five and helped him reach a new personal rating peak. Photo: Maria Emelianova In November and December 2024, Gukesh faced Ding Liren in the World Championship match in Singapore. The contest began with a setback for the Indian, who lost the first game with the white pieces. However, he responded with remarkable composure, demonstrating the resilience and fighting spirit that had characterised his rise to the top. The match remained balanced as the two players traded blows. Everything came down to the 14th and final game. In a dramatic endgame, Gukesh capitalised on a mistake from his opponent and secured victory by the narrowest of margins, 7.5–6.5. At just 18, he became the youngest undisputed World Champion in chess history, breaking a record that Garry Kasparov had held for more than four decades. Photo: Eng Chin An With this extraordinary achievement, Gukesh became India’s second world chess champion after Viswanathan Anand and emerged as an inspiration for a new generation of players, both at home and around the world. Throughout his rise, Gukesh has consistently displayed a growth-oriented mindset. Even after capturing the world title, he made it clear that winning the championship was not the ultimate destination, but rather another milestone on his journey. He openly acknowledged that there was still much to learn before he could establish himself as the world’s strongest player. The period that followed, however, proved considerably more challenging than expected. Having reached the pinnacle at such a remarkably young age, Gukesh appeared to encounter the first significant plateau of his career. Since around the middle of 2025, his results have been increasingly inconsistent, with a series of disappointing performances affecting his position among the world’s elite. He has since slipped to 26th place in the FIDE rating list, with 2710 Elo points. For a reigning World Champion, such a decline inevitably raises questions about confidence, form and the ability to withstand the pressure that comes with defending the ultimate title. Gukesh now faces the difficult task of rediscovering the form that made him virtually unstoppable during his remarkable 2024 campaign. The next chapter of Gukesh’s career will unfold against an opponent who is also young, ambitious and exceptionally talented. Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan has enjoyed a spectacular rise over the past year, winning the 2025 World Cup before dominating the Candidates Tournament in April 2026. His qualification for the Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026 sets the stage for a fascinating clash between two players representing the new generation of elite chess. Both have already demonstrated their ability to compete at the highest level, but they arrive at the match from very different positions. While Sindarov will be eager to seize his first opportunity to become World Champion, Gukesh must prove that he can rediscover his championship-winning form and withstand the unique pressure of defending the crown. The old saying goes that defending a title is often more difficult than winning it in the first place. For Gukesh, the challenge is arguably even greater: he must overcome not only a formidable opponent but also the recent struggles that have interrupted his progress. title: Sahel Chess Festival: Bringing the world of chess to Africa
summary: It would be difficult to decide what was more exciting at the second edition of the Sahel Chess Festival: the late-summer heat and the beach just outside the hotel, the splendid excursions, the friendships formed among players from twenty federations, or the chess itself. Most rooms of the official hotel, the four-star El Habib  (https://elhabib.hotelmonastir.net/en/) look out onto its grounds and beach  More than 300 participants gathered in Monastir, Tunisia, from 25 to 31 October for the second edition of the Sahel Chess Festival. The event demonstrated that the first edition had been a brave and good move. Its repeated success this year suggests that the festival is well on its way to reaching even greater heights.     The buzz in the comfortable playing hall just before the start of the first round The Sahel Chess Festival is run under the auspices of the Tunisian Chess Federation and FIDE. The African Chess Confederation’s Vice President, IA and IO Wajdi Chouari, attended the closing ceremony. The Festival featured five classical tournaments, played over nine rounds using the Swiss system: Open A, “Élite” (Elo 2000 and above); Open B, “Ascension” (1700–1999); Open C, “Progression” (1500–1699); Open D, “Rising Stars” (below 1500); Open E, “The Path of the Wise”, reserved for seniors aged 50 and above and an Open Blitz tournament. Chief Arbiter, IA-B Mohamed Ali Baktache (seated, third from left) with his team Sambuev takes the crown Bator Sambuev is a Canadian Grandmaster originally from Ulan-Ude, the capital of Buryatia, a Russian republic in south-central Siberia. In June 2007, he immigrated to Canada and subsequently represented his adopted country at two Chess Olympiads: Istanbul 2012, where he played on first board, and Tromsø 2014, on fourth board. He has won the Canadian national championship four times. Arriving in Monastir as the top seed, Sambuev never relinquished his leading position. He went on to win the tournament unbeaten with a round to spare, scoring an impressive 8/9. His only concessions were two draws, against IM Mohamed Ali Boudriga (TUN) and FM Nicolo Casadio (ITA). From the sixth round onwards, 18-year-old Egyptian IM Wafa Hamed emerged as Sambuev’s closest pursuer. However, having lost their direct encounter, he remained a point behind the leader and eventually secured second place. Wafa is one of the most promising young talents in African chess. A chess prodigy, he is the reigning African Junior Champion in the Under-20 category, having won the title for the third consecutive year. He also represented Egypt at the latest Chess Olympiad. Chess talent clearly runs in the family: his two older sisters, Shrook and Shahenda, are both Women Grandmasters and highly accomplished players, having won the African Women’s Chess Championship multiple times. Half a point behind Hamed, Italian IM Valerio Carnicelli claimed third place. Carnicelli was part of a four-player Italian delegation. He was accompanied in Monastir by FM Nicolo Casadio, WFM Giulia Sala and Valeria Martinelli. Casadio is Italy’s reigning national Youth Champion. IM Zaur Tekeyev (2424, FID) missed the podium, finishing half a point short. He nevertheless had something to celebrate: victory in the Open Blitz, where he scored 8/9. IM Zaur Tekeyev, winner of the Blitz tournament, with Tournament Director Miladi Chaher Tunisian triumph in Open B In Open B, two home-grown players claimed the top two places. Eighteen-year-old Badr Bilel Chabchoub took the lead in the fifth round and never looked back. He finished with an outstanding 8.5/9, adding 75 points to his rating.    The runner-up, Chady Dahmen, had initially been hovering in the middle of the standings, among several players on the same score. However, a remarkable winning streak in the final five rounds propelled him into second place. He finished with 7/9 and gained an impressive 151 rating points. Libyan player Reda Saleh Aldrsi completed the podium with 6.5/9. Open B winner and runner-up: Badr Bilel Chabchoub and Chady Dahmen Russian GM Alexander Raetsky gave a 20-board simultaneous exhibition in the hotel’s sunny courtyard. Local talent Thabet Benzarti attracted the spectators’ attention by skilfully steering his game to a draw. Young Indian talents are regular participants in international open tournaments. At the Sahel Festival, India was represented by 12-year-old CM Aryan Mehta, who travelled with his coach, GM Farrukh Amonatov (2575, TJK). Amonatov took the opportunity to play in the Open Blitz, where he scored 7/9. Young player and coach: CM Aryan Mehta and GM Farrukh Amonatov The mysterious “Mr X” https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P1kocV97-Yo was revealed as Dutch FM Ramon Koster, who competed in Open A and scored 5.5/9 An international open tournament offers much more than the opportunity to measure one’s strength against players from other countries. For many participants, it is a chance to earn their first international rating, gain valuable rating points or achieve a title norm. WIM Margarita Potapova (2225, FIDE) has particularly good reasons to remember the Sahel Festival fondly. Fresh from winning the Russian Women’s Blitz Championship, which had concluded just days before her arrival in Monastir, she continued her winning streak. She finished as the best woman in the tournament, placed sixth overall in Open A and, with a performance rating of 2401, secured a WGM norm! A festival for the next generation International open tournaments are magnets for young players everywhere, particularly in places where such opportunities are relatively scarce. Boys and girls travelled with their parents from all corners of Tunisia and from abroad. For many, it was their first experience of an international tournament, and several succeeded in earning their first international rating. More than 50 young players were under 16. Of the 45 female participants, 15 were under 16.  Festival sponsor and organiser Hassen Abdelaali with Maram Mami, the best girl U-10 and a “Smarty” (the affectionate nickname given to students of the Smart Chess Academy) The Smart Chess Academy in Sousse practically closed its doors during the festival, as most of its students headed to Monastir to put their newly acquired skills to the test. title: Aaron Nimzowitsch: 140 years since the birth of a chess pioneer
summary:
Born in Latvia, Aaron Nimzowitsch was one of the most important players and theorists of the first third of the 20th century, influencing generations of chess players with his strategic ideas. His life, however, was far from easy and sadly cut short. Today marks the 140th anniversary of his birth. | Photo: J. Graudenz

140 years since the birth of Nimzowitsch

Aaron Nimzowitsch was born on 7 November 1886 in the Latvian capital, Riga. The family name was originally Ņimcovičs in Latvian, meaning roughly "son of the German". In its Germanised form, it was written Niemzowitsch, with the stress on the penultimate syllable. At some point, when a passport was issued, the "e" disappeared and the stress shifted to the first syllable.

At the time of Nimzowitsch's birth, Latvia was a province of the Russian Empire. Aaron Nimzowitsch learned chess at the age of eight from his father, Isaja Abramovich, a wealthy Jewish timber wholesaler who was himself a good chess player. Aaron Nimzowitsch's exceptional talent for chess became apparent very early. His first games were published in a Riga newspaper when he was only nine years old, and were subsequently reprinted in other chess publications. The family later moved to Dvinsk (now Daugavpils), where Nimzowitsch attended a Talmud school.

Aaron Nimzowitsch with his sister Tilla and his father Isaja (Schaja) | Photo source: Batgirl on chess.com

In 1903, Nimzowitsch went to Berlin intending to study philosophy. Instead, however, he devoted more of his time to chess and regularly visited the Café Kaiserhof, where Berlin's chess players gathered at the time.

In October 1903, he enrolled in Göttingen to study mathematics and psychology, but returned to Berlin after one semester. In 1906/07, Nimzowitsch was also enrolled in Zurich to study mathematics, though he did not complete that course either. After several successful tournament appearances, Nimzowitsch finally decided to make chess his profession and abandoned his studies for good.

Nimzowitsch played his first tournament in Coburg, where the 14 th Congress of the German Chess Federation was held in 1904. Nimzowitsch competed in the main tournament and finished a respectable sixth in a strong field. Tournaments in Vienna and Barmen followed, and he even managed to win an event in Munich. By May 1907, Nimzowitsch was already among the participants in the major international tournament in Ostend. Twenty-nine players competed for almost six weeks, and the 20-year-old Aaron Nimzowitsch was among the leaders. He eventually shared third-fourth place with Jacques Mieses, behind Ossip Bernstein and Akiba Rubinstein. Within three years, Nimzowitsch had reached the world's elite. In August/September 1907, the leading European players gathered in Carlsbad. Nimzowitsch finished a strong joint fourth-fifth, sharing the position with Carl Schlechter. Rubinstein won the tournament.

After that, however, Nimzowitsch disappeared from tournament play for three years. He had withdrawn from several tournaments he had agreed to play in during 1908. During this period, he stayed in Riga. In his biographical notes for a new edition of My System , Jacques Hannak suggested that Nimzowitsch was working on his new strategic ideas. Perhaps, however, his temporary withdrawal had another reason. Nimzowitsch's biographers Per Skjoldager and Jørn Erik Nielsen ( Aron Nimzowitsch: On the Road to Chess Mastery, 1886–1924 , McFarland, 2012) report that the first signs of tuberculosis may already have appeared in 1908. In later years, repeated references were made to Nimzowitsch suffering from health problems.

Aaron Nimzowitsch (c. 1916) | Photo source: Per Skjoldager and Jørn Erik Nielsen ( Aron Nimzowitsch: On the Road to Chess Mastery, 1886–1924 , McFarland, 2012)

Nimzowitsch reappeared in 1910 and, until the outbreak of the First World War, played in a number of top tournaments: the Masters tournament at the 17 th DSB Congress in Hamburg in 1910 (third place), Carlsbad in 1911 (fifth-sixth), and the tournaments in San Sebastián in 1911 and 1912 (sixth-eighth and second-third respectively). In 1912, Nimzowitsch played in the All-Russian Championship in Vilnius, finishing fourth.

In the qualifying tournament for the great international Masters tournament in Saint Petersburg in 1914, Nimzowitsch shared first place with Alexander Alekhine, who was six years younger. As the playoff also ended without a winner, both players were admitted to the international Masters tournament in April/May 1914. Nimzowitsch finished eighth in the preliminary stage.

On 1 August 1914, the First World War began, fundamentally changing the political landscape and economic conditions in Europe. Information about Nimzowitsch's life during this period is rather vague. He was probably in Riga when the war began. In 1916, he is said to have been conscripted into the military.

Following the February Revolution of 1917, the Tsar abdicated on 15 March 1917. The subsequent attempt to establish a parliamentary democracy failed in the face of the Communists, who continued the revolution, particularly in rural areas. In the summer of 1917, the last major Russian offensive against the Central Powers failed at the front.

Lenin had returned to Russia in April 1917, led the Bolshevik movement and advocated an end to the war. In November 1917 (October according to the old Julian calendar), the Bolsheviks overthrew the bourgeois government. German troops had occupied Riga in September 1917.

Nimzowitsch, by then apparently discharged from the Russian military, worked for a time as chess editor of the Baltische Zeitung . Afterwards, there was reportedly another attempt to conscript him by force. According to some anecdotes, he avoided this by pretending to be mentally disturbed. It has also been reported, however, that Nimzowitsch may have been in Berlin in 1917 under the name Arnold Nimzowitsch. Perhaps he escaped the military authorities by fleeing. A number of casual games and simultaneous exhibition games played by Nimzowitsch in Riga from 1918 to 1920 have survived.

On 3 March 1918, the new Bolshevik rulers in Russia signed a peace treaty with the German Empire under which Russia was forced to make extensive territorial concessions. Following the Treaty of Versailles, the political balance of power also changed in Eastern Europe, and the Russians now attempted to revise the treaty with the German Empire and regain control of lost territories, including the Baltic region. Between 1918 and 1922, Russia was also ravaged by a civil war that lasted until the founding of the USSR and claimed eight million lives.

In these turbulent times, Nimzowitsch decided to leave his homeland for good. In July 1920, he went to Stockholm and in August played in the Gothenburg Chess Club jubilee tournament (12 th out of 14 participants; Réti won ahead of Rubinstein). In October, he took part in the Stockholm Chess Club jubilee tournament (second behind Bogoljubow). In 1921 and 1922, Nimzowitsch played smaller matches and gave several simultaneous exhibitions in Norway and then Denmark. The Copenhagen Chess Association had invited him to Denmark. Nimzowitsch gave lectures and played games against Danish players to promote chess in the country.

In November 1922, Nimzowitsch moved permanently to Denmark and lived until his death in a room at Øster Farimagsgade 11 (on the second floor) in Copenhagen.

At the beginning of the 1920s, chess life in Europe slowly began to recover and reconnect with the great era before the First World War. Nimzowitsch was a frequent guest at the major tournaments, usually competing near the top and achieving good results. He was even able to win some events. In Carlsbad in 1923, he finished sixth in a field of 18. In Baden-Baden in 1925, he finished ninth out of 21. In Mariánské Lázně in 1925, he won ahead of Rubinstein and Marshall.

At the DSB Congress in Breslau in the summer of 1925, he finished second behind Bogoljubow. He came fourth at the 1926 Semmering tournament, where he scored, among other results, a victory over Alexander Alekhine. Nimzowitsch won the jubilee tournament in Dresden in April 1926, finishing ahead of Alekhine. His game against Johner is perhaps Nimzowitsch's most famous game.

Nimzowitsch also won the jubilee tournament in Hanover in August 1926, this time finishing ahead of Rubinstein.

The partcipants of the 1926 Hanover tournament. Back row: Friedrich Sämisch, Oskar Hans Antze, Hans Duhm, Walther von Holzhausen. Front row: Aaron Nimzowitsch, Hermann von Gottschall, Jacques Mieses, Akiba Rubinstein.

Nimzowitsch was invited to a tournament in New York in February 1927 and finished third behind Capablanca and Alekhine. The tournament was played over four rounds. Nimzowitsch failed to win a game against Capablanca, but he did manage to defeat Alekhine once.

Back in Europe, he played tournaments in 1927 including Berlin (second place), Kecskemét (winner), Bad Niendorf (winner) and London (winner). In 1928, Nimzowitsch also won the Berlin Chess Society jubilee tournament. At Bad Kissingen, he finished fifth in a world-class field.

The players in Bad Kissingen | Photo source: Douglas Griffin on X

He finished second behind Capablanca in the Berliner Tageblatt tournament.

In 1929, Nimzowitsch won the new edition of the Carlsbad tournament with an outstanding 15 points from 21 rounds, finishing ahead of Capablanca and many other world-class players. At Alekhine's dominant performance in San Remo in 1930, Nimzowitsch finished second as the "best of the rest".

Nimzowitsch v. Grau | Photo: via Douglas Griffin on X

He finished second in Liège and won the Anderssen jubilee tournament in Frankfurt.

In 1931, he won a tournament in Switzerland and finished third in the strong tournament at Bled. No games at all are known from 1932. He then played tournaments and matches in Denmark, and his participation in the 1934 tournament in Zurich (sixth-seventh) effectively marked the end of Aaron Nimzowitsch's international career. In August 1934, he played his final tournament at the Nordic Congress in Copenhagen.

In his retrospectively calculated ratings, Jeff Sonas ranks Aaron Nimzowitsch as world number two behind Akiba Rubinstein in 1913 and as world number three, behind Alekhine and Capablanca, between 1926 and 1931.

The style of his games and Nimzowitsch's behaviour both at and away from the chessboard struck some colleagues and contemporaries as unusual. There are several anecdotes describing his sometimes peculiar behaviour. It was reported, for example, that in Hamburg in 1910, after Köhnlein played 1.e4, Nimzowitsch initially did not react at all. He stared at the board for several minutes, then at his fingers. He then stood up and looked at pictures on the wall before reading a brochure advertising a new chess clock. Eventually, he made a move. In another game, he arrived 45 minutes late but showed no urgency to move, again looked at a few pictures on the wall, then made a move while standing shortly before the default time expired, only to return immediately to the pictures. He also played his next moves quickly in passing and soon nevertheless obtained a winning position.

Above all, however, Nimzowitsch tried to ensure that at least at his own board nobody smoked. Burning tobacco leaves and inhaling the smoke was a widespread habit at the beginning of the 20 th century, including among chess players. Once one knows that Nimzowitsch suffered from a lung condition, however, his aversion to tobacco smoke becomes understandable, even though his contemporaries did not appreciate it. Nimzowitsch's fragile health may also explain some of his unusual behaviour. At times, he appeared irritable and nervous, probably when his health was poor.

The unorthodox way he conducted his games also irritated the other masters, particularly the highly dogmatic Siegbert Tarrasch. As early as 1913, however, Nimzowitsch had launched a frontal attack on Tarrasch in a characteristically undiplomatic article. Tarrasch subsequently criticised Nimzowitsch's style of play on various occasions and described his openings as "ugly". The two masters never became friends and conducted an intense and public war of words in contributions to chess magazines.

title: The young king faces his toughest challenge
summary:
Gukesh Dommaraju will defend his world title against Javokhir Sindarov in Geneva after a remarkable rise that made him the youngest undisputed champion in history. Since his 2024 triumph, however, the Indian grandmaster has endured a more difficult period and slipped down the world rankings. The match therefore presents a different challenge: rediscovering his best form while facing a younger rival who arrives with strong recent results and considerable momentum. | Image: FIDE

Press release by FIDE

From prodigious talent to the youngest world champion in history, Gukesh Dommaraju has enjoyed a meteoric rise to the summit of the chess world. Now, as he prepares to defend his crown against Uzbekistan's rising star Javokhir Sindarov, the Indian prodigy faces perhaps the greatest challenge of his career: rediscovering his best form.

World champion Gukesh Dommaraju embodies ambition, determination and youthful excellence. His remarkable rise to the pinnacle of the chess world, marked by record-breaking achievements and historic milestones, is an extraordinary story of talent, perseverance and self-belief. At just 18 years of age, he achieved what generations of chess players can only dream of: becoming the youngest undisputed world champion in history.

Born on 29 May 2006 in Chennai, the same city that nurtured India's chess legend Viswanathan Anand, Gukesh showed signs of exceptional talent from an early age. Having learned the rules of chess at the age of seven, he quickly demonstrated a natural aptitude for the game, winning the Asian School Chess Championships in 2015. Soon afterwards, he left formal schooling to devote himself entirely to chess.

With the unwavering support of his parents, Gukesh continued to develop his skills, becoming an international master in 2017. His training approach placed particular emphasis on independent thinking and understanding positions rather than relying on chess engines. This helped him develop a distinctive playing style and strong analytical abilities. In January 2019, at the age of just 12 years, 7 months and 17 days, he became the second-youngest grandmaster in chess history.

Photo: John Saunders

His progress continued at an impressive pace. After collecting medals at international youth championships, Gukesh spent the Covid period further strengthening his game, and competed both online and over the board. Another breakthrough came at the 2022 Chess Olympiad in Chennai, where he represented India's second team, helping it secure the bronze medal. Individually, he produced a spectacular performance on the first board, scoring 9 points out of 11 and winning the individual gold medal.

Further outstanding results in 2022 and 2023 propelled him into the world's elite. He became the youngest player ever to surpass the 2750 Elo rating mark and qualified for the 2024 Candidates Tournament. Held in April, this prestigious competition brought together eight of the world's strongest players to determine the challenger to reigning world champion Ding Liren. Gukesh once again made history by becoming the youngest Candidates' winner ever.

Photo: Michal Walusza

September 2024 brought another landmark achievement for Indian chess. At the Chess Olympiad in Budapest, India claimed its first-ever gold medal. Gukesh played a central role in this historic triumph, winning the individual gold medal on board one with an outstanding score of 9 points out of 10 and a stellar rating performance of 3056. This result also propelled him into the world's top five and helped him reach a new personal rating peak.

In November and December 2024, Gukesh faced Ding Liren in the World Championship match in Singapore. The contest began with a setback for the Indian, who lost the first game with the white pieces. However, he responded with remarkable composure, demonstrating the resilience and fighting spirit that had characterised his rise to the top. The match remained balanced as the two players traded blows.

Everything came down to the fourteenth and final game. In a dramatic endgame, Gukesh capitalised on a mistake from his opponent and secured victory by the narrowest of margins, 7½–6½. At just 18, he became the youngest undisputed world champion in chess history, breaking a record that Garry Kasparov had held for more than four decades.

Photo: Eng Chin An

With this extraordinary achievement, Gukesh became India's second world chess champion after Viswanathan Anand and emerged as an inspiration for a new generation of players, both at home and around the world.

Throughout his rise, Gukesh has consistently displayed a growth-oriented mindset. Even after capturing the world title, he made it clear that winning the championship was not the ultimate destination, but rather another milestone on his journey. He openly acknowledged that there was still much to learn before he could establish himself as the world's strongest player. The period that followed, however, proved considerably more challenging than expected. Having reached the pinnacle at such a remarkably young age, Gukesh appeared to encounter the first significant plateau of his career. Since around the middle of 2025, his results have been increasingly inconsistent, with a series of disappointing performances affecting his position among the world’s elite. He has since slipped to 26 th place in the FIDE rating list, with 2710 Elo points.

For a reigning world champion, such a decline inevitably raises questions about confidence, form and the ability to withstand the pressure that comes with defending the ultimate title. Gukesh now faces the difficult task of rediscovering the form that made him virtually unstoppable during his remarkable 2024 campaign.

The next chapter of Gukesh's career will unfold against an opponent who is also young, ambitious and exceptionally talented. Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan has enjoyed a spectacular rise over the past year, winning the 2025 World Cup before dominating the Candidates Tournament in April 2026.

His qualification for the Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026 sets the stage for a fascinating clash between two players representing the new generation of elite chess. Both have already demonstrated their ability to compete at the highest level, but they arrive at the match from very different positions. While Sindarov will be eager to seize his first opportunity to become world champion, Gukesh must prove that he can rediscover his championship-winning form and withstand the unique pressure of defending the crown.

The old saying goes that defending a title is often more difficult than winning it in the first place. For Gukesh, the challenge is arguably even greater: he must overcome not only a formidable opponent but also the recent struggles that have interrupted his progress.

In recent months, the Indian champion has reportedly sought time for reflection and preparation, with his visit to the Tirumala Temple in Andhra Pradesh in early November attracting attention. Whatever role such moments of introspection may play, there is little doubt that Gukesh will be determined to give himself every possible chance of success. There is no doubt that he possesses all the ingredients required to mount a successful title defence. His opening versatility, exceptional calculating ability, resilience under pressure and fearless approach to complicated positions remain major strengths. Above all, his ability to rise to the occasion has already been demonstrated on the biggest stages, from the Candidates Tournament to the final game of the 2024 World Championship match.

Photo: Michal Walusza

For Gukesh, the Geneva match will be about much more than retaining the world title. It will be an opportunity to reaffirm his place among the very best, silence doubts about his recent performances, and demonstrate that his historic triumph in Singapore was the beginning of a new era rather than the peak of a brief but extraordinary journey.

title: Bavarian Championship: Sasikiran joins Gopal in the lead
summary:
With 6 points from 7 rounds, Indian grandmasters Krishnan Sasikiran and G.N. Gopal share the lead at the Bavarian Chess Championship in Tegernsee. Their opponents' average ratings of 2413 (Sasikiran) and 2411 (Gopal) also leave them closely matched on tiebreaks, with both having faced stronger opposition on average than any other participant. Gopal drew with Elham Amar on the top board. While the games on the neighbouring boards also ended in draws, including Frederik Svane (5½/7) against Adrian Gschnitzer, Sasikiran secured a win over Rithvik Raja. | Photo: Sandra Schmidt

Two co-leaders, two rounds to go

After round seven, the Bavarian Championship is led by the two Indian GMs, Krishnan Sasikiran and G.N. Gopal. Gopal was able to maintain his advantage over most of his direct pursuers, as the games on the first five boards all ended in draws, but Sasikiran scored a win against his compatriot Rithvik Raja and was able to move into shared first place. Sasikiran and Gopal are therefore both on 6 points and lead the standings.

Frederik Svane drew with black on board two against Adrian Gschnitzer. With 5½ points, Frederik Svane is only half a point behind the leaders before the penultimate round on Saturday. Leonardo Costa drew with Roven Vogel, while Alexander Donchenko defeated Moritz Weishaeutel to join Frederik Svane and Leonardo Costa. In total, 21 players are on 5½ points.

The two highest-placed women are Maria Tsakona (47 th ) and Kateryna Dolzhykova (49 th ), both on 5 points.

Adrian Gschnitzer and Frederik Svane | Photo: Sandra Schmidt

Adrian Gschnitzer v. Frederik Svane

In his game against Frederik Svane, Adrian Gschnitzer managed to obtain an advantage. In the endgame, he captured a pawn with check, and it was precisely this move that gave Frederik Svane the opportunity to get back into the game and hold the draw.

At this point, there was already a material imbalance. Gschnitzer had a rook, bishop and five pawns, while Svane had two rooks and three pawns. After 45.Bxe5+ Kg8 46.Bf6 Rxe4+ , Black had enough activity with his rooks to win or exchange all but two of White's pawns. In the end, they agreed to a draw.

In this endgame, Frederik Svane showed plenty of patience and held out in a complicated position long enough to reach an equal position again. In the final position, he could still have captured the b-pawn, but neither side could see a way to win.
